title: How Do We Remember?
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · Memorials as works of art

hero.credit: Dietmar Rabich, *Berlin, Denkmal für die ermordeten Juden Europas -- 2011 -- 2415*. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

objective: Students will look closely at the memorials whose photographs the exhibition shows — in Berlin, Treblinka, the Rzuchów Forest, Warsaw, Kyiv and Prague — and at the exhibition’s own Walk and memorial stone. They will describe each by its **material, shape and scale, words** and what it asks of **the visitor**, compare two, and design a memorial of their own with a short **artist’s statement**.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: A memorial is a work of art with a duty: to remember real people truthfully. Looking closely at how artists have met that duty shows us how remembering works.

items.text: describe a memorial by its material, shape, scale and words, and say what each choice makes a visitor feel or do

materials: *The memorials in this lesson* on page 3, projected; drawing pencils
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** walk *The Walk*, where the iron faces and empty shoes sound under your feet, and *Lay a Stone* on the memorial stone. Open *Look closer* on the timeline to read more about each memorial here.

steps.title: What is this place?
script: Project the photograph with no title. *“What do you notice? How might it feel to walk between these blocks? What might this place be for?”* Take ideas. Then name it: the **Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe**, in Berlin. Ask: *it has no names and no pictures — how does it remember?*

img.credit: Dietmar Rabich, *Berlin, Denkmal für die ermordeten Juden Europas -- 2011 -- 2415*. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

screen.alt: Rows of plain grey concrete blocks of different heights on cobbles
screen.caption: Berlin

steps.purpose: Look before knowing: let the form speak first.
students: How might it feel to walk between these blocks?
What might this place be for?

steps.title: Six memorials
script: Show six memorials (page 3), one at a time, and read what the exhibition tells us of each: the **field of stones** at Treblinka, many carrying a town’s name; the long memorial in the **Rzuchów Forest**, whose word PAMIĘTAMY means “We remember”; Natan Rapoport’s **Monument to the Ghetto Heroes**, unveiled in Warsaw on April 19, 1948; the **menorah** at Babyn Yar; the **blue glass wall** at Tiergartenstraße 4; and the **empty library** under the cobbles of Bebelplatz, which recalls the book burnings.

steps.purpose: See that each memorial remembers in its own way.
students: What is each one made of?
Which uses words? Which uses none?
Which would you most want to stand beside?

steps.title: Four questions
script: Give the four questions: **material; shape and scale; words; the visitor.** Practice them together on one memorial.

screen.caption: Four questions to ask of any memorial

cells: Material. What is it made of, and why?
Rough stones at Treblinka; blue glass in Berlin; iron in the Walk
Shape and scale. How big? How many parts?
Hundreds of stones; rows of concrete blocks of different heights
Words. Does it name, explain, or stay silent?
PAMIĘTAMY, “We remember”; the walls of names in Prague
The visitor. What does it ask you to do?
Walk among it; look down through glass; lay a stone

steps.purpose: Learn four questions to ask of any memorial.
students: Ask the four questions of one memorial.

steps.title: Names, and stones
script: Close with two memorials that ask something of us. In Prague, the names of the murdered cover the synagogue’s walls; the exhibition notes that Yad Vashem has found five million of the six million names. And: *Many Jewish visitors place a small stone on a grave or memorial to show that someone has come and that the person is remembered. A stone lasts where flowers fade.* The exhibition’s own **Walk** is inspired by Menashe Kadishman’s *Fallen Leaves* and the *Shoes on the Danube Bank*.

steps.purpose: See how a memorial can name, and can invite the visitor to take part.
students: Why write every name you can?
Why does a stone last where flowers fade?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. Every level ends with a design sketch and a short statement.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Look closely at three memorials with *I see / I think / I wonder*, then design a remembrance stone for the classroom, choosing its material, shape and one word, with a sentence frame for the statement.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare two memorials with the four questions, then sketch a memorial and write a 50–70 word artist’s statement.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Weigh two hard choices — names or no names, and who a memorial includes (Babyn Yar, 1976 and 1991) — then propose a memorial with a statement that defends its choices.

steps.purpose: Look, compare and design at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. Every level ends with a memorial of your own design.

steps.title: Gallery walk
script: Lay the designs out as a gallery. Students walk in silence and leave one note by a design: *what does it ask the visitor to do?* Read two notes aloud.

screen.question: Walk the gallery in silence. Leave a note by one design: what does it ask the visitor to do?

steps.purpose: Look at each other’s designs as visitors would.
students: Leave one note: what does this design ask the visitor to do?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
